ComprehensionText:
The crystal clear, blue water and the magnificent sun make the Caribbean island of Saint Maarten a favorite vacation spot, one that is popular with North Americans during their winter holidays from December through March, as well as with South Americans and Europeans from April through August. The French and Dutch settled on the island in the 1600s, and to this day, the island is divided between the two of them. The French capital is Marigot; the Dutch capital is Philipsburg.

Tourists soon discover that St. Maarten has an intriguing history. Ancient artifacts found on the island date back to the Stone Age, 6,000 years ago! Tourists also learn that 1,200 years ago the Arawak

7 2 Indians inhabited all the islands of the West Indies and were a peaceful people living under the guidance of their chiefs. Three hundred years after the Arawaks first arrived on St. Maarten, in the 1300s, they were defeated and forced to abandon the island by a hostile tribe of Indians originating in South America. This new tribe was called the Carib. The Caribbean Sea was named after them. Unlike the Arawaks, they had no permanent chiefs or leaders, except in times of strife. And they were extremely warlike. Worse, they were cannibalistic, eating the enemy warriors they captured. In fact, the very word cannibal comes from the Spanish name for the Carib Indians. The Spanish arrived in the fifteenth century and, unfortunately, they carried diseases to which the Indians had no immunity. Many Indians succumbed to common European illnesses; others died from the hard labor forced upon them.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Ivar and the flying fish

Ivar's new method of fishing had exceeded all expectations. Never in the history of their small Viking community had such an enormous number of fish been caught in less than one hour, and by a 12-year-old boy—albeit an intellectually gifted one. Ivar calculated his catch to be the finest on record. This 'finest on record' catch, however, presented a slight problem: how to preserve 756 herrings really quickly.

Ivar immediately applied his considerable intellect to solving the problem.

He went to his favourite thinking place, overlooking the fjord. The wind was brisk and icy. It whistled up the fjord; it always did as winter attempted to reassert its authority over spring. The icy water of the fjord below rippled in response to the tugging winds just as an idea tugged at Ivar's thoughts. He grabbed a piece of bone and sketched a rough diagram in the dirt. His new idea was inspired by a wooden propeller he had designed for the family boat some years earlier; it had long since been used as firewood. Ivar considered that the wind might do the work of rotating the propeller blades. His fish would be tied to the blades and, in the blustery conditions of early spring, would be very efficiently wind dried!

Ivar was buzzing! He thrived on the inspiration-to-implementation of the design process. His precious elk horn collection would provide the material for the blades and a recently felled tree would make a sturdy vertical post. Ivar was busy!

Hours later, as dusk fell and the residents prepared their evening meals, a strange thudding noise was heard on nearly every mud roof in the village. Those villagers who had timber roofs described the sound as closer to a 'strange clattering noise'. Either way, there was something peculiar happening that evening.

High above the village, in his beloved (but currently very windy) thinking place, Ivar had a different problem. He was struggling to keep the fish tied to the blades of his turbine-type machine. The device worked too well—currently it was rotating at 15 revolutions per minute even with 150 or so medium-sized fish strapped on—and threatened to lift off its hillside perch. He had lost at least 60 fish in the last few minutes, and who knew where they had landed?
QuestionText: When the writer comments about winter's attempt 'to reassert its authority over spring', she means that
AnswerA: the weather conditions were unusual for spring.
AnswerB: winter is a much harsher season than spring.
AnswerC: the weather in early spring can still be cold.
AnswerD: spring is a much shorter season than winter.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Thirty Languages in Cooma
Anna's first word of English was 'snow', and she learned it the week her family arrived in Cooma in the winter of 1952.
Her father had come from Norway six months earlier to work on the Snowy Mountains Scheme, the enormous project to build dams, tunnels and power stations in the mountains of New South Wales. Now Anna, her mother and her baby brother had followed him across the world. From the bus window, Cooma looked small and wind-swept, with rows of new houses and muddy streets. But on the main street, Anna heard more languages in five minutes than she had heard in her whole life: Italian, German, Polish, Greek, Dutch and others she couldn't name.
'Men from more than thirty countries,' her father told her. 'All here to bring water and electricity to Australia.'
School was the hardest part. On her first morning, the teacher, Mrs Hartley, wrote 'Welcome Anna' on the blackboard and pointed to a seat next to a girl with dark plaits. The girl was called Lucia, and she was from Italy. She knew only a few more English words than Anna, but she smiled and pushed half of her pencils across the desk.
For weeks the two girls spoke in a mixture of English, pointing and drawings. Lucia taught Anna 'playground' and 'lunch'. Anna taught Lucia how to make a snow angel. When Mrs Hartley asked the class to draw where their fathers worked, the girls discovered that their fathers were digging the same tunnel, one from each end.
In the evenings, Anna's father came home grey with rock dust, so tired he sometimes fell asleep at the table. Anna's mother worried, but her father always said the same thing: 'One day you will switch on a light, and some of that power will come from our mountain.'
By spring, Anna could read simple books in English. She still spoke Norwegian at home, but at school she sometimes forgot which language she was using until she saw Lucia laughing.
Years later, when the tunnel was finished, the two families stood together at the opening ceremony. Anna and Lucia, now taller than their mothers, held hands as the water rushed through the mountain their fathers had joined.
QuestionText: In the story, the word 'wind-swept' means . . .
AnswerA: covered in deep snow
AnswerB: exposed to strong winds
AnswerC: freshly swept and clean
AnswerD: crowded with people

Anna's first word of English was 'snow', and she learned it the week her family arrived in Cooma in the winter of 1952.

Now Anna, her mother and her baby brother had followed him across the world. From the bus window, Cooma looked small and wind-swept, with rows of new houses and muddy streets. But on the main street, Anna heard more languages in five minutes than she had heard in her whole life: Italian, German, Polish, Greek, Dutch and others she couldn't name.

Dear Diary,

The dust storm has been blowing for nine sols, so outdoor walks are cancelled, the windows are brown, and the only thing on the learning screen was a lesson about air filters. AIR FILTERS. I live in a dome where the air is filtered every second of every day. I think I know about air filters.
Then, after lunch, Commander Osei made an announcement. The cargo lander that touched down before the storm had brought something special, and everyone was to meet in the Green Bay at fifteen hundred hours.
The Green Bay is where we grow lettuce, tomatoes and beans under pink lights. It always smells damp and a bit like socks. Today it was packed. Right in the middle, in a big pot, stood a tree.
Okay, it was not a big tree. It was about as tall as me, with a thin grey trunk and maybe forty leaves. The label said Eucalyptus, which Dad says is from Australia, where he grew up. But it was a TREE, Diary. A real one, not a picture or a hologram.
Here's the strange part. The adults who were born on Earth went very quiet. Mrs Petrova put her hand over her mouth. Dad crouched down, crushed a leaf between his fingers and breathed in, and his eyes went shiny. He said it smelt like a summer holiday he had when he was nine.

It smelt sharp and clean, like medicine, but alive. It didn't remind me of anything, because I don't have any summer holidays on Earth to remember. Still, my chest felt tight, in a good way.
The botanists say that if the tree survives, its seeds could one day grow a whole grove inside the new dome. I asked if I could help look after it. Dr Ahmed said yes, on Thursdays.
So now I have a job. Tree Keeper, Ares Dome. The storm is still blowing, but I don't mind so much any more.
Leo

Let the Mall Sing
Walk through our town mall on a Saturday morning and what do you hear? The beep of a pedestrian crossing, the rumble of delivery trucks and perhaps a crying toddler. What you will not hear is music. Since the council introduced strict new rules last year, buskers have almost vanished from our streets. I believe these rules should be relaxed, and street performers welcomed back.
Under the current rules, buskers must buy a permit costing one hundred dollars, perform only in two small marked squares beside the car park and finish by eleven o'clock in the morning. For a teenager hoping to earn a little pocket money with a guitar, that is a steep price for a spot that hardly anyone walks past.
Street music brings life to a town. A violinist playing outside the bakery makes people slow down, smile and linger. When shoppers linger, they spend. Shop owners in many other towns have found that a lively street draws more customers, not fewer. Music is an invitation; silence is a shrug.
Busking also gives young performers a stage. Not every talented musician can book a concert hall. Some of Australia's best-known performers began by playing on footpaths, learning to win over people who had not come to hear them. That is a tough audience, and it builds skill and confidence quickly.
Finally, buskers make music free for everyone. A concert ticket can cost more than many families can afford. On the street, a child can stop and watch a juggling drummer for as long as they like, and pay nothing more than a clap.
Of course, the council has reasons for its rules. Some shopkeepers complained about performers who were too loud or who played the same three songs all day. These concerns are fair. But the answer is not to drive buskers away; it is to set sensible limits. A cheap permit, a volume limit and a rule that performers move spots every two hours would solve most problems without silencing anyone.
Our mall was built for people, and people have always gathered around music. Let's change the rules, unpack the guitar cases and let the mall sing again.

AnswerA: hurry away

AnswerD: complain loudly

The year is 1150 BC. The location is a meadow not far from Stonehenge in Britain.

'Are we all present?' boomed Drystan, the 'leader' of our little band, while adjusting his lately acquired deerskin cloak which he wore as his symbol of leadership.

Eleven voices murmured agreement and one asked, 'Is this a birthday party?'

'No laughter in the stone circle' Drystan tried to boom again while undoing the bone toggle of his cloak which was threatening to constrict his breathing.

'The purpose of our meeting today is to discuss design ideas for a small shelter so we can have our meetings in all weather conditions, Drystan informed us.

'We could use a few animal skins stretched over a timber frame,' I suggested.

'That's a dumb idea, Anyou, Drystan intoned.

Clearly, praise and encouragement were aspects of leadership that Drystan needed to develop further.

'We will build our shelter using stone,' stated Drystan.

'Yes, Drystan. Of course, Drystan,' we all chimed.

All day we collected stones, piling, wedging and balancing them until we had a shelter that looked like it had been designed by a landslide. Still, it seemed to please Drystan and that's all that mattered really. The last job of the day involved rolling an extra large log near the entrance to the shelter. Drystan would use this as his podium when he was directing his horde of followers.

Dutifully we pushed the designated log in the approximate direction of the shelter. The remaining events are listed in our (secret) meeting records as follows:

1. After a bit of a push, the log gathered speed as a result of a slight incline.
2. The log took off on its own accord and proceeded (quickly) in a northerly direction towards Stonehenge.
3. The log came to rest against a stone pillar at the entrance and the pillar was dislodged.
4. Large stones fell like dominoes around the circle that was Stonehenge.
5. In unspoken agreement we all left the scene immediately. Drystan had a head start on all of us.

A few months later I overheard a conversation among the village elders as to the cause of the Stonehenge catastrophe. One voice was louder than the rest: 'An unusual alignment of stars in combination with a rainbow and an easterly wind!' I recognised it as the voice of Drystan's father. The other elders nodded their agreement. Drystan must have inherited his father's leadership skills, I concluded, because they both have strong voices.
QuestionText: According to Anyou, why was Drystan the leader?
AnswerA: He had the loudest voice.
AnswerB: He had the cleverest ideas.
AnswerC: He had a father whom the children feared.
AnswerD: He had been given a symbol of leadership.
